written_by_H027.Excerpt1: “I just cain't wrap my head 'round it, Ennis. Just give it to me straight up: you want me around or don't ya? Cause this here between us ain’t anything in full, and because it ain’t anything in full it ain’t hardly anything at all. All we see of each other is here, alone with ourselves. I only got you here. Out there, you ain’t anybody I ever known. All we got here are moments on Brokeback Mountain, and moments ain’t a life, ain’t close to living. How much more of ourselves are you willing to let die? Don’t you know how much less of me I feel of myself? You keep all that I am on the shortest leash, Ennis. You are the one keeping us from the fullness of what our lives could be. Maybe you can keep on like this, but I can’t. I’m at the end of that rope. God, Ennis. I want to quit you. I wish I knew how to quit you.” Nearing the tailend of these words Ennis’s knees buckled, his body softened, as if having taken birdshot to his backside, though to Jack any outer wound could not be found. Jack went silent then, and kept it, unsure what to do with Ennis screaming, “Jesus, Jesus…” And though Ennis calmed, and the air on the mountain steadied, nothing had changed. Still they would go on as they had before, no one in the world knowing what they had between them, except them. The pain on that mountain would go on with them, too, would follow them into the days and weeks ahead, so weighty, like clouds of steam rising between the two.
written_by_H027.Excerpt2: Jack said what he said every time: "I'm tellin' you this one time, and I ain't foolin'. What I want—know why we're here? I want to know why, if I'm up in Lightning Flat in December and you're down in Texas maybe come June, why the hell can't I meet you somewhere in between for a few days? Hell, count them few times we been together in the same damn place. I got a gutful of it, enough. I'm done bein' dumb about this, see? When the hell we gonna get a chance to get it right? We been a fuckin' pair! And you know damn well what I'm sayin'. Damn you, Ennis del Mar. Brokeback Mountain—we kill ourselves up there. That's all we've got. Damn you. You've got me on a short leash, hung me up for years. Sometimes I miss you so much I can hardly stand it. I wish I knew how to quit you." Tears were running down Jack's face.Like vast, powerful haymakers, these words were blows that knocked a man down without warning. Ennis sagged to his knees seeking  to catch his breath. "Jesus," said Jack, thinking the man was having a heart attack as he knelt beside Ennis on the poured slab, putting his arm around his shoulder. Once the shock had passed Ennis hauled himself to his feet, flinched away from Jack, turned his back to him, and tried to be calm. He lit a cigarette, unbuckled his belt, and pulled his shirt out of his jeans. Nothing changed except who they were and what they felt—a silence that rose between them like clouds of steam.

written_by_H027.Original: “Try this one,” said Jack, “and I’ll say it just one time. Tell you what, we could a had a good life together, a fuckin real good life. You wouldn’t do it, Ennis, so what we got now is Brokeback Mountain. Everything built on that. It’s all we got, boy, fuckin all, so I hope you know that if you don’t never know the rest. Count the damn few times we been together in twenty years. Measure the fuckin short leash you keep me on, then ask me about Mexico and then tell me you’ll kill me for needin it and not hardly never gettin it. You got no fuckin idea how bad it gets. I’m not you. I can’t make it on a couple a high-altitude fucks once or twice a year. You’re too much for me, Ennis, you son of a whoreson bitch. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Like vast clouds of steam from thermal springs in winter the years of things unsaid and now unsayable—admissions, declarations, shames, guilts, fears—rose around them. Ennis stood as if heart-shot, face grey and deep-lined, grimacing, eyes screwed shut, fists clenched, legs caving, hit the ground on his knees.“Jesus,” said Jack. “Ennis?” But before he was out of the truck, trying to guess if it was heart attack or the overflow of an incendiary rage, Ennis was back on his feet and somehow, as a coat hanger is straightened to open a locked car and then bent again to its original shape, they torqued things almost to where they had been, for what they’d said was no news. Nothing ended, nothing begun, nothing resolved.

Jack had more to say but his jaw stayed shut. Ennis sobbed. After awhile he went still. Ennis pulled himself to his feet and pushed the dust off his jeans. Jack looked at him and Ennis looked back, but there was nothing there. Just the clouds of steam rising.

written_by_H027.Excerpt1: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.
written_by_H027.Excerpt2: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.
written_by_H027.Reason: Excerpt 1 is closer to the original in voice and style. It matches the calm, reflective tone and controlled emotion of the original better than Excerpt 2, which feels more active and emotionally charged. Both of these excerpts are very similar to the original and difficult to separate, but the first is closer.
written_by_H027.Original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.

written_by_H023.Excerpt1: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings. An umbrella tumbled along the shoreline, and a plastic bag drifted past me. A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.

written_by_H014.Excerpt1: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

written_by_H052.Excerpt1: I breathed in the night air that might or might not have smelled like blossoms. Looking at the incomparable skyline of Manhattan, I felt a familiar thrill - one I'd never been able to explain, though I knew it came from seeing those tiny illuminated windows set against the massive forms that contained them.The thrill was so intense and singular that it must have been more than just the visual relationship, for apart from a cityscape, nothing natural or man-made held my attention long enough to provoke it. What I saw, I thought, was a material form of the second person plural, the true subject of art. It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. I'd long felt that one wanted to be an artist to make bad forms of collectivity appear as the promise of an almost unimaginable good: not reified abstraction, poorly disguised negation of the one in the many, but the emerging collective that would do justice to the wrongs absorbed by the bodies below the skyline. Tonight the fiction of the world—all my strongest perceptions, including rare fictions of participation in a benevolent collectivity—had gathered around Noor as if she were a black hole. Through her I was being changed more fully into a thing, a person among persons, and the experience was only horrible to the extent that it wasn't total. The uncanny feeling of not being identical with yourself, of being a stranger to your own experience, is profoundly alienating, yet it holds a glimmer of utopian hope. This sense of dislocation is available to be felt as a rearticulation, a promise that the past can be unlocked in the present. It is the paradoxical hope that in the moment you realize you are not yourself, you experience the possibility of becoming another, allowing the past to be reconfigured, rewritten in the now.I thought all this at midnight on a cheap folding bench with my hair flattened by a bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, tearing up a little—a mild lacrimal event—projecting myself into this scene from the future.
written_by_H052.Excerpt2: The scent of blossoms colors the night, and New York in its entirety fits very neatly and completely into my hands. For instance, between my thumb and my index, lights flicker on and off in a miniature window. If I elongate my fingers I could also hold the silver skyscrapers tearing into the clouds. How astonishing; the skyline’s ants and beasts fit right, and wrong, into my palms. Back in my father's village nothing, absolutely nothing, fit into my hands. There were no neat edges anywhere, no contrast, nothing for me to want to try to hold. In short, there is no place I feel less alone than here, alone on this bench in New York, where the skyline is ours, and we are the skyline, my eyes staring straight into the material manifestation of a second person plural. In the future, they will say this skyline was synonymous with every art, every intimate form that has ever, or will ever, exist. To say we are the skyline is to confirm a collective identity, to confirm a stake in what makes up the city's sublime marrow; bundled debt, traces of antidepressants in the water, traffic networks, and shifting weather patterns. As an artist it will be my mission to transmute bad forms of collectivity into a sculpture of the communal body of the future. There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. So maybe we multiply, keep multiplying, and our past and present and future selves never leave, and maybe that is what Noor really meant when she said the world has no genre you can name. The midnight air does nothing to unflatten my hair beneath the bandana. I would mistake this moment for a dream if I had not just consumed an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice all over my fingers. I vaguely remember a dream of myself as an old man, maybe an old woman, my fingers free of both tiny windows and the stain of fruit, and with this memory of the future I experience a mild lacrimal event, and I feel very alone, and very together.

written_by_H022.Excerpt2: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?

written_by_H022.Original: I breathed in the night air that was or was not laced with anachronistic blossoms and felt the small thrill I always felt to a lesser or greater degree when I looked at Manhattan’s skyline and the innumerable illuminated windows and the liquid sapphire and ruby of trafﬁc on the FDR Drive and the present absence of the towers. It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

written_by_H022.Excerpt1: I breathed in the night air that might or might not have smelled like blossoms. Looking at the incomparable skyline of Manhattan, I felt a familiar thrill - one I'd never been able to explain, though I knew it came from seeing those tiny illuminated windows set against the massive forms that contained them.The thrill was so intense and singular that it must have been more than just the visual relationship, for apart from a cityscape, nothing natural or man-made held my attention long enough to provoke it. What I saw, I thought, was a material form of the second person plural, the true subject of art. It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. I'd long felt that one wanted to be an artist to make bad forms of collectivity appear as the promise of an almost unimaginable good: not reified abstraction, poorly disguised negation of the one in the many, but the emerging collective that would do justice to the wrongs absorbed by the bodies below the skyline. Tonight the fiction of the world—all my strongest perceptions, including rare fictions of participation in a benevolent collectivity—had gathered around Noor as if she were a black hole. Through her I was being changed more fully into a thing, a person among persons, and the experience was only horrible to the extent that it wasn't total. The uncanny feeling of not being identical with yourself, of being a stranger to your own experience, is profoundly alienating, yet it holds a glimmer of utopian hope. This sense of dislocation is available to be felt as a rearticulation, a promise that the past can be unlocked in the present. It is the paradoxical hope that in the moment you realize you are not yourself, you experience the possibility of becoming another, allowing the past to be reconfigured, rewritten in the now.I thought all this at midnight on a cheap folding bench with my hair flattened by a bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, tearing up a little—a mild lacrimal event—projecting myself into this scene from the future.
written_by_H022.Excerpt2: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?

written_by_H014.Excerpt1: We sit and watch Aunt Sara and Elizabeth as they walk slowly back and forth through the gymnasium, their skirts making the sound of waves as they scrape against the floor. We want to move, but we are afraid of the cattle prods, because we have seen what they do to others, the way bodies twist under them like writhing serpents, the way skin burns where the prods touched them for days after. We watch the Angels, too, guards who gaze into the distance as though they are somewhere else, far away. We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. We imagine a world where we beg for our freedom, for the chance to go outside, into the egg-colored sun, to step barefoot on the wet grass, to spin in the cool wind of the day. We imagine what it would be like to leave the cold, fetid horror of this place behind, let it become a memory, a vile, coppery taste at the backs of our throats. But we know better than to go to them. They are the ones with loaded guns, which they hold cradled in their arms like babies. We’ve seen what has happened to the girls who dare to speak to the Angels, the heaviness of a body when it falls to the floor after it’s been penetrated with a bullet, the deafening and definitive crack of the gunshot. For now, we sit and we watch. We stay still and we dream and we yearn. We wait and we imagine something other than the rigid darkness of today.
written_by_H014.Excerpt2: The smell of the wood chips on the floors of the caged gymnasium where we slept, that stale, sweet odor; the moist sheen of bundled bodies, carried with us into the sunlight. I remember that yearning, that thirst for something we could never grasp. It wasn't just the touch of tongues and fingers, of sweaty thighs; it was a desire for the future. It was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep. We created so many illusions for ourselves, of one kind or another. How else could we live? I remember whispering as we folded laundry late at night, those soft, slow voices moving through the humid air. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the end of the beds. In the semidarkness we could stretch out our arms, when the Aunts weren't looking, and touch each other's hands across space. We learned to lip-read, our heads flat on the beds, turned sideways, watching each other's mouths. In this way we exchanged names, from bed to bed: Alma. Janine. Dolores. Moira. June.The door was locked, and it was forbidden for us to be awake in here after lights-out. We were constantly being watched. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods worn on leather belts, but no guns. Guns were for guards, a.k.a. Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when they were bringing new women or taking the old ones away. They stayed outside, with their backs deliberately turned toward us. They were objects of fear, but familiarity dulled our apprehension. What we fantasized about more than anything else was the possibility of touching them, or having them touch us, using our bodies as the currency, the ultimate coin of exchange—what we would give them for freedom. There was nothing we wouldn't give.
written_by_H014.Reason: The 2nd excerpt is closer in my opinion because it has a softer and more reflective feeling, which allows the reader to connect with it far easier than the first. The language used matches the original's tone, whereas the first excerpt feels like it is being retold. The first also leans too heavily on metaphor.
written_by_H014.Original: There was old sex in the room and loneliness, and expectation, of something without a shape or name. I remember that yearning, for something that was always about to happen and was never the same as the hands that were on us there and then, in the small of the back, or out back, in the parking lot, or in the television room with the sound turned down and only the pictures flickering over lifting flesh.We yearned for the future. How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? It was in the air; and it was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep, in the army cots that had been set up in rows, with spaces between so we could not talk. We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.

written_by_H018.Excerpt1: Look. I've been the one making the plan, and I want to be the one to execute it. There was a silence before she spoke again. I'll be honest, I'm not the kind of person who's so crazy about living that I want to put off dying as long as I possibly can. I'll be ready. In fact, I'm already impatient. But like I told you, no one can be sure how the cancer's going to behave. We all know there are sometimes surprises, and the body can be very stubborn about giving up, and it's always possible that treatment might be delayed. And I want this as natural as possible. I want to be in a certain state. I don't want to be in distress. I don't want to be rescued. I don't want my hand held. I'm sorry, but I just can't commit to any particular moment, any particular day. It could happen tomorrow. It could happen in a couple of weeks. As the saying goes, it'll be like the coming of the Lord. You won't know the day or the hour. But don't worry, she added, feeling the words catch in her throat. You'll know the minute afterward. Remembering my full mailbox, I said I'd want my mail held if I went away for a week or more. She pressed her lips together and frowned. I had gone too far. The truth was, it was unthinkable for me to bring all this up at all. I'd rather you didn't mention the drug, or how I got it, to anyone. You understand, don't you? For your own protection—and for mine. But this promise I had already broken. I had already shared this information with someone.
written_by_H018.Excerpt2: I remember things. I remember how I felt when my friend talked about taking her own life. She wasn’t planning to commit suicide exactly. But she wanted her life to come to an end, she said. Her honesty made me pause and I wondered what I should do in such a situation. Could I make her change her mind? Would I have to look after her things and live with guilt? It would’ve been different if my friend didn’t want to handle “her situation” on her own terms. She, who had always been a planner, had even decided which drug she wanted to use to die, and asked me to keep it a secret, both for her sake and for my “protection,” whatever that meant. What concerned me though was that she wanted to do it soon. She said it slowly and calmly, but her tone was riddled with impatience and readiness. My friend had been ill for a long time and her body had not been responding well to treatments. She had spent so much in hospitals that now she wanted death to feel natural, without any interventions or disruptions. Smooth and clean. She hoped death would arrive like an unexpected guest. “Like the coming of the Lord, you know?” she said, with a laugh. I was in two minds. I wanted to know when she was planning for it all to go down, but it felt unthinkable to probe directly about her timeline. And, I felt equally concerned with more practical issues. If I were to stay with my friend during her final days, my mail would pile up. What would I do then? And what would happen to everything she had? It was all this and more about her, including her choice of pill, that I recounted to another friend of mine later in the day.

written_by_H051.Excerpt1: I was invited to lunch by a billionaire who wanted to start a literary magazine. The London club was opulent, the atmosphere carefully crafted through gilded light fixtures and dark accents. I was late, carrying my heavy suitcase and sweating, but the billionaire wore casual clothes and seemed unbothered by my lateness, launching into an explanation of his software project for predicting employee betrayal. The literary journal had not come up when the waitress brought bread to us, nor when she brought a range of appetizers. I realized the billionaire had ordered for us both. He insisted then on paying for a taxi to the airport, a generosity I would not decline given the rush of my morning. As we ate, he unfurled his life story. ‘It’s all what you’d expect,’ he said. ‘Rags-to-riches, you know—to be rich and unbothered, that’s the real achievement. To feel calm,’ he told me. ‘That’s what it allows.’ I wondered if he thought of the literary magazine as an entry point into writing. Everyone wants to write, I’ve noticed; everyone imagines themselves a writer, even if they have never put pen to paper. The billionaire had funded a good many ambitious ventures. A floating wind farm with worker houses, and something about a scheme to eliminate lawyers for managing personal matters. The waitress brought small plates, caviar and shaved truffle and mint suspended artfully over a scallop. The billionaire played drums in a rock band to relax. He was expecting his eleventh child, a number of children he knew and hoped that I would balk at, and explained that four of his children were adopted Guatemalan quadruplets. The waitress came along with another round of drinks. A perfect cube of ice sat in the center of each. I was struggling to process most of what the billionaire had said, the dishes before us becoming more and more luxurious, and expensive. His frenetic, scattered storytelling and sweet enthusiasm felt childlike against the opulence of our experience, of this lunch. When he put me in my taxi, he said ‘Enjoy yourself in Athens.’ This surprised me, as I didn’t recall telling him my destination. Actually I could not remember saying anything during our lunch.
written_by_H051.Excerpt2: A billionaire once invited me to lunch at his club in London. He was very keen to show me his latest software project, which was a program that could predict which employees in a company would next betray their boss. I had to catch a plane immediately afterwards and so was a little restless, and he insisted on paying for my taxi to the airport, which was nice, since I'd come with a suitcase. We were supposed to be talking about a literary magazine he wanted to start, and I hadn't expected his personal security software to come up. But when we sat down and started, it was he who told me the story of his life. I assembled the biography: a humble beginning, the lessons in work and intellect, and finally this  tawny-haired and surprisingly well-muscled figure at the table across from me. I guess he imagined that the literary magazine might provide some sort of entrée into the practice of writing, seeing as he'd got and done pretty much everything else with his money. He told me a lot more – about the complexity and immensity of his entrepreneurial schemes, such as a floating wind farm that would house and provide credit for its workers and thereby solve the problem of world poverty and ecocide; or another scheme he had for legally disposing of lawyers from people's personal lives. He also mentioned that he'd taken up playing drums in a rock band every Thursday night, because why not; and that he was presently expecting his eleventh child, counting the Guatemalan quadruplets he and his wife had adopted earlier. The billionaire talked for so long that I couldn’t keep up with it all, I was almost too exhausted to follow. Waitresses kept arriving, removing dishes and bringing huge plates of lobster and bottles of fine wine. His focus was so scattered, his enthusiasm so limitless, it was almost like that of a child. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, putting me in the taxi afterwards, though I didn't remember mentioning I was going there.

written_by_H055.Excerpt1:
"Well, life's dealt some rather unkind cards. One son, a pukka Englishman—a suit-wearing, diploma-carrying, Tory-voting coward—while my other son has gone from muttering one-liners about infidels to a bloody fundamentalist terrorist. I can't say it surprises me. Yes, I made a devil's pact; yes, yes—but please tell me where was the better option? My father, from whom I could never escape, made quite sure there was only one road to be taken. To hell with it. This is the suffering of the immigrant: of my generation and Archibald's, immigrants by necessity, English by residence but not by birth. For us first-generation folk, those who came here fleeing hardship, there is always the struggle to make a home, a real home, in what remains another's land."

"Oh, that's not true, surely," murmured Irie helplessly.

"It's very much the truth, I'm afraid. The worst of it is, you see, this time spent in the belly of the beast. Two years become four, four becomes eight, then twelve. For so many of us, it is far too late to go back. Better to give up the very idea of belonging. I truly tried to give my children roots and culture and language and traditions, but all I have succeeded in giving them is the sickness of the immigrant, the curse of the stuck-in-between. But at the same time, I can't forget what I lost. Balance, my friend. Balance."
written_by_H055.Excerpt2: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." He was not sure why he was telling this to the waiter, because he couldn't tell if it was real ash or maybe just little crumbs from the tea itself."Oh dear, I'm sorry sir. I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.

The perspective in which the story is told in the original matches better with excerpt one. Excerpt two uses a lot more first person perspective compared to excerpt two and the original excerpt.
written_by_H055.Original: "There are no words. The one I send home comes out a pukka Englishman, white suited, silly wig lawyer. The one I keep here is fully paid-up green bow-tie-wearing fundamentalist terrorist. I sometimes wonder why I bother," said Samad bitterly, betraying the English inflections of twenty years in the country, "I really do. These days, it feels to me like you make a devil’s pact when you walk into this country. You hand over your passport at the check-in, you get stamped, you want to make a little money, get yourself started. but you mean to go back! Who would want to stay? Cold, wet, miserable; terrible food, dreadful newspapers — who would want to stay? In a place where you are never welcomed, only tolerated. Just tolerated. Like you are an animal finally house-trained. Who would want to stay? But you have made a devil’s pact... it drags you in and suddenly you are unsuitable to return, your children are unrecognizable, you belong nowhere." "Oh, that’s not true, surely." "And then you begin to give up the very idea of belonging. Suddenly this thing, this belonging, it seems like some long, dirty lie... and I begin to believe that birthplaces are accidents, that everything is an accident. But if you believe that, where do you go? What do you do? What does anything matter?"

written_by_H004.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_H004.Excerpt2: When I was in college I joined the Black Panther Party. I wore a black turtleneck sweater and black beret and stood outside in the cold with arms full of old newspapers. I wasn’t trying to prove my ideological stance. I was trying to prove that I was indeed Black. It seems that no one, Black or white, thought I was Black enough. Once when a loose ball was bounding about on a basketball court, I muttered “Egads,” and people’s heads turned. When I savored a biscuit and described it as sublime, I received odd looks. And, of course, I was not nearly gloomy or angry enough as a writer. Of a retelling of Aeschylus, a reviewer wrote: “The novel has some merit, but do we really need this from a Black man?” A literary agent puffed up with plastic pride told me at a New York party that nobody wanted an intellectual Black man, especially one doing retellings of Greek plays. I pointed out that I actually knew Greek. He laughed and asked if that was a joke and suggested I should write some true, gritty real stories of Black life instead. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories. I was sure that he had no idea what I was talking about.He sniffed at the air, feigned boredom and proceeded to chat up the Afro woman, who I heard later was a performance artist. I knew I was Black, saw myself as Black, but race was a fiction. A handy one, a stupid one, a dangerous one, but a fiction nonetheless. To be honest I don’t think about race much, except when my liberal guilt compels me to consider it or when I read about some thirteen-year-old kid being shot by some cop, and then I remember that though race is a construct without a basis in the natural world, those bullets are quite real and deadly.

written_by_H004.Original: While in college I was a member of the Black Panther Party, defunct as it was, mainly because I felt I had to prove I was black enough. Some people in the society in which I live, described as being black, tell me I am not black enough. Some people whom the society calls white tell me the same thing. I have heard this mainly about my novels, from editors who have rejected me and reviewers whom I have apparently confused and, on a couple of occasions, on a basketball court when upon missing a shot I muttered Egads. From a reviewer: "The novel is finely crafted, with fully developed characters, rich language and subtle play with the plot, but one is lost to understand what this reworking of Aeschylus’ The Persians has to do with the African American experience.".One night at a party in New York, one of the tedious affairs where people who write mingle with people who want to write and with people who can help either group begin or continue to write, a tall, thin, rather ugly book agent told me that I could sell many books if I’d forget about writing retellings of Euripides and parodies of French poststructuralists and settle down to write the true, gritty real stories of black life. I told him that I was living a black life, far blacker than he could ever know, that I had lived one, that I would be living one. He left me to chat with an on-the-rise performance artist/novelist who had recently posed for seventeen straight hours in front of the governor’s mansion as a lawn jockey. He familiarly flipped one of her braided extensions and tossed a thumb back in my direction.The hard, gritty truth of the matter is that I hardly ever think about race. Those times when I did think about it a lot I did so because of my guilt for not thinking about it. I don’t believe in race. I believe there are people who will shoot me or hang me or cheat me and try to stop me because they do believe in race, because of my brown skin, curly hair, wide nose and slave ancestors. But that’s just the way it is.

Despite my being a Black writer, the book was, apparently, not written from a Black perspective. At the latest New York literary party, a well-known literary agent told me, "You should forget those retellings of yours; classical works aren't what the market is looking for. The agent shuffled past me to attend to a performance artist so they could see what they could do for one another, before never speaking to each other again.I didn't know how to contend with any of it: how to portray myself as "Black enough," the backward, ill-feeling guilt behind not being so, and how to fit into the mold that society made of Black men. We all had to be gangsters, rappers. But why should I have been anything other than who I was? Race was a construct I didn't believe in and rarely dwelt on, until those moments arose when guilt compelled me to see the "other side" of the matter. I saw its real-world consequences: police brutality, discrimination, violence. I didn't know if that meant I was supposed to take part in any of it.

written_by_H055.Excerpt1: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.

I pointed out that I actually knew Greek. He laughed and asked if that was a joke and suggested I should write some true, gritty real stories of Black life instead. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. written_by_H049.Excerpt1: It was early winter already, and once it got dark the room was piteously cold. While there was still light, my mother got up and went into the kitchen. She filled the biggest rice bowl with water, then put it on the gas burner and waited for it to come to the boil. She snipped a length of white thread from the spool in her sewing box, and gently pressed a small pair of scissors into the steaming water. When the pain became so insupportable that she could no longer stand up, she lay down in the middle of the room. Labor began at around midnight. Trembling with fear, she used a scrap of white cloth to swaddle the newborn, as thin as a rat, and tied the thread around the barely pulsating umbilical cord. Then she severed it. She held the baby to her breast and murmured, Live, please live. Go on living and become my son. She continued to murmur to herself even as its barely open eyes closed for the final time. Go on. Keep going. After that, silence. The cold from the earthen floor invaded her back. Soaked into and through her flesh. Matching her lifeless child.
written_by_H049.Excerpt2: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no. With shaking hands, she fashioned a gown from loose fabric she kept tucked away in her sewing box. As though the faux-hospital garb could imbue the experience with a semblance of professionalism. The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.

written_by_H049.Original: It was early winter, the first frost of the year. My 22-year-old mother crawled into the kitchen and boiled some water to sterilise a pair of scissors. Fumbling in her sewing box, she found some white cloth that would do for a newborn’s gown. Gripped by contractions and terribly afraid, tears started down as she plied her needle. She finished the tiny gown, found a thin quilt to use as swaddling bands, and gritted her teeth as the pain returned, quicker and more intense each time.Eventually, she gave birth. Still alone, she cut the umbilical cord. She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made, and held the whimpering scrap in her arms. For god’s sake don’t die, she muttered in a thin voice, over and over like a mantra. After an hour had passed, the baby’s tight-sealed eyelids abruptly unseamed. As my mother’s eyes encountered those of her child, her lips twitched again. For god’s sake don’t die. Around an hour later, the baby was dead. They lay there on the kitchen floor, my mother on her side with the dead baby clutched to her chest, feeling the cold gradually leach into the flesh, sinking through to the bone. No more crying.

written_by_H028.Excerpt1: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."
written_by_H028.Excerpt2: The restaurant was an annex to the Trois-Couronnes.I had a pale face and was wearing my spectacles that day, which made me look sad. That wasn't the issue, though. My father and I had been seated at the table reserved for groups, on the far side of the dining room, and were ignored throughout the meal. At the next table, there was a man with his daughter, who was older than I was, maybe seventeen, sleek and tanned with short blonde hair. I remember a long, gilt-framed mirror hanging above their heads, reflecting endless repetitions of identical people. The girl talked confidently to her father and laughingly spooned up her yogurt. In those days, I didn't know what yogurt was. She seemed at home, oblivious to her surroundings, wearing no jacket or headscarf, simply her checkered summer dress. She made me feel awkward and ashamed, although I couldn't explain why, my only desire being to leave as soon as possible. Later on, walking along the streets, my father kept saying, "Those mashed potatoes looked like pig slop." For the first time, I realized that he had been marking time to continue, repeating the reason why he hadn't eaten anything on his plate. I didn't think of asking him what difference it made what the potatoes looked like. Deep down, he was upset at being treated as a second-class customer just because we weren't dining "à la carte" like the people sitting near us.

Like the original, it blends internal reflection with external detail, especially through imagery and the subtle contract between the storyteller and the girl. Excerpt two is more analytical and less intimate in tone and voice.
written_by_H028.Original: One evening ‒ it was our last day ‒ in Tours, we had dinner in a brightly-lit restaurant where the walls were lined with mirrors, frequented by a sophisticated clientele. My father and I were seated at the end of a long table set up for the group. The waiters were paying little attention to us; we had to wait a long time between courses. At a small table nearby sat a girl aged fourteen or fifteen, suntanned, in a low-cut dress, and an elderly man who appeared to be her father.They were talking and laughing quite freely, completely at ease, oblivious of other people. She was dipping into a thick milky substance in a glass ‒ some years later I learnt this was yogurt, which people like us had never heard of. I caught sight of myself in the mirror, pale and sad-looking with my spectacles, silently sitting beside my father, who was staring into the far distance. I could see everything that separated me from that girl yet I wouldn’t have known what to do to resemble her.Afterward, my father complained with unusual vehemence about this restaurant, where he claimed we had been served mashed potatoes made with “pig slop,” white and tasteless. Several weeks later, he was still venting his anger over the meal and its disgraceful “pig slop.” Although he never actually said so ‒ it was probably then that I began decoding his speech ‒ it was his way of expressing resentment at having been treated with contempt because we were not chic customers who ate “à la carte.”

written_by_H065.Excerpt1: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”
written_by_H065.Excerpt2: That year, at Christmas, my father gave me three crisp hundred-dollar bills instead of a gift. He invited me to join him and Chitra and Rupa and Piu at Disney World, where they were planning to spend part of the girls' winter vacation. I told him I couldn't go because school started up again the day after New Year's, but I didn't tell him that I checked the calendar first and realized that we would be back in plenty of time. To make up for it, I bought my half sisters ridiculously expensive presents—a record player for Rupa and a camera for Piu. Rupa cried when I told her I wasn't going to Disney World, which was where the record player and camera would be put to use. Piu put her arms around me. "I don't understand you, Didi," she said, still in her small, high voice. "What did we do wrong that makes you not want to go?" The truth was that in my eyes they had done nothing wrong, whereas I was punished by their mere existence. But I was still convinced that it was up to me to honor my mother's memory, just as they instinctively honored the man who was their father but not really mine. Still, I sensed that Chitra was relieved by my decision, and, by extension, so was my father.

written_by_H065.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father did not try to persuade me. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.

Father told me that day: “I am proud to have a daughter like you.” Then he added that he had nothing to say to me, nothing at all. That evening, Mother showed me a photograph taken forty years before, when my father had just got his degree: he had large brown eyes and a full head of silver hair that stood up above his head. “I can’t stand this,” she said quietly. “It is intolerable. written_by_H054.Original: On my last visit, my father seemed in worse condition than I had seen him before. When I asked him if he was working on anything in particular now, he said no and then turned his head slowly to my mother and looked at her in bewilderment, his mouth hanging open. My mother asked me to admire his pajamas, and he stood quietly while I did. Then he said: “I don’t know what I will be like in the morning.” After he went to bed, my mother showed me a picture of him forty years before sitting at a seminar table surrounded by students. “Just look at him there!” she said in distress, as though it were some sort of punishment that he had become what he was now—an old man with a beaked profile like a nutcracker.

written_by_H052.Excerpt1: I barely recognized my father when I entered the kitchen, which was probably because he completely failed to recognize me. All my life I had felt only he knew my name. I was a stranger to everyone else, even to my mother, whose voice had repulsed me ever since I was a girl. I probably should not have said this, but I was relieved when I realized I was not the only fact of his life he forgot. "What was I when I was?" he asked my mother in the kitchen. She ran to the bookcase. "You wrote this all yourself," she told him, extra nasally. "It was a Bible on the Bible. A seminal take-down of anti-Semitism." I could tell he was not listening. Then suddenly he turned to me. Suddenly I was me again. When he said my name I returned to my skin. "What are you?" he asked me, and when I told him, his eyes filled with something I recognized. "If I had any words left I'd spend them on voicing just how proud I..." he stuttered before a long pause. "I have nothing to say," he whispered. Night fell again. When he went to sleep in the kitchen I was not sure he would wake up, but my mother decided tonight was a fine time to dig up their 40-year-old wedding pictures. "He is a gorgeous man," she said, then yawned the word "was."

written_by_H016.Excerpt1: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between craving something and fulfillment. Sometimes I want something so much I feel like I’m going to break open. Let’s say it’s a fresh berry, let’s say it’s like I’ve been really wanting a fresh berry, plucked from a bush in the orchard, even before that berry’s in my hands, it’s already got a taste in my mind, I’ve been building it up moment after moment until I have it in my brain like I’ve already got it on my tongue, so when Sylvie tells me she picked something for me and plops it in my mouth, it’s even sweeter because the sweetness confirms the foundation I’ve already built for it. I don’t know how to put it. Sylvie disappeared for a while, like a mouse, but then she came back. Sometimes she still goes out though, vanishes into the woods without saying anything. I think she’s out there right now, watching me ruminate. I don’t know what kind of solitude we can both get when we both are in each other’s minds. Could it be a way of being together? A very strange way? It’s beautiful out in the woods. The trees are older than I can fathom, really, old like stories can be old. I’d like to put a status out there, almost like somebody would always be watching, a statue of a woman, to stand in between all those old trees, a woman in a crown of new flowers, looking only ever ahead, forward, never letting any kind of barrenness touch her, like she was the opposite of Lot’s wife and all there was to her was the kind of forgiving vibrancy that children wonder at, the vibrancy that comes from a life well-lived. Even as a statue, I think they’d come to her, every child that’s ever felt lost-wild and orphan, and I think when they’d reach out to touch her stone hands, they’d find that that statue’s stone was warm for them. Sometimes I wish Sylvie were warmer. There’s warmth all around in all the beautiful trees and even the grasses. The problem is that trees don’t feel warm when you touch their bark unless it’s from the sun.
written_by_H016.Excerpt2: Craving and its indulgence are really one and the same thing. There might be no fruits, and still, if one wished for them, yearned for them, one would taste them all. The very sight of a berry in the wild is an admonishment not to pick it, for when it is stored in the vision and played upon by desire, the taste it bears is gifted to it as much by memory as by its savor. The flavor grows until it is too exquisite for the tongue, unencumbered by flesh. So it is when one wishes for a friend, or a woman, or a child. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The wind was dying, the sun was sinking, the side of the house was cooling, the evening moths were glancing and settling, and her absence was a thing so full of longing it became a presence of its own. If I could row the lake at dawn and gather all the proud blossoms from the woods for one year, I would throw some across the graves of unsanctified and dreamless children and some into the holes of fox dens. And with the rest I would sculpt from snow a statue of a woman. I would stand her in the clearing in the woods, and she would be adorned with rare flowers with leaves like hands, with hardstem thistles, and the birds would rest in her. Lot's wife would have none of this: flowers in profusion and children. Her breast caved into a hollow of regret. Not this one, not my mother. All the wild children, who knew too well that the world does not give itself generously to children, would burst from the trees and behold her. And every child, the most orphaned, the most bereft, would forgive her for her frozen hands and would stand at her white hem in awe that she should seem to shower them with blossoms, eternally offering what she could never give, inexplicably so stern.

written_by_H016.Original: To crave and to have are as like as a thing and its shadow. For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it, and when is the taste refracted into so many hues and savors of ripeness and earth, and when do our senses know any thing so utterly as when we lack it? And here again is a foreshadowing—the world will be made whole. For to wish for a hand on one’s hair is all but to feel it. So whatever we may lose, very craving gives it back to us again. Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries.Sylvie was gone. She had left without a word, or a sound. I thought she must be teasing, perhaps watching me from the woods. I pretended not to know I was alone. I could see why Sylvie thought children might come here. Any child who saw once how the gleaming water spilled to the tips of branches, and rounded and dropped and pocked the softening shadows of frost at the foot of each tree, would come to see it again.If there had been snow I would have made a statue, a woman to stand along the path, among the trees. The children would have come close, to look at her. Lot’s wife was salt and barren, because she was full of loss and mourning, and looked back. But here rare flowers would gleam in her hair, and on her breast, and in her hands, and there would be children all around her, to love and marvel at her for her beauty, and to laugh at her extravagant adornments, as if they had set the flowers in her hair and thrown down all the flowers at her feet, and they would forgive her, eagerly and lavishly, for turning away, though she never asked to be forgiven. Though her hands were ice and did not touch them, she would be more than mother to them, she so calm, so still, and they such wild and orphan things.

The flavor grows until it is too exquisite for the tongue, unencumbered by flesh. So it is when one wishes for a friend, or a woman, or a child. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The wind was dying, the sun was sinking, the side of the house was cooling, the evening moths were glancing and settling, and her absence was a thing so full of longing it became a presence of its own. If I could row the lake at dawn and gather all the proud blossoms from the woods for one year, I would throw some across the graves of unsanctified and dreamless children and some into the holes of fox dens. And with the rest I would sculpt from snow a statue of a woman. I would stand her in the clearing in the woods, and she would be adorned with rare flowers with leaves like hands, with hardstem thistles, and the birds would rest in her. Lot's wife would have none of this: flowers in profusion and children. Her breast caved into a hollow of regret. Not this one, not my mother. All the wild children, who knew too well that the world does not give itself generously to children, would burst from the trees and behold her. And every child, the most orphaned, the most bereft, would forgive her for her frozen hands and would stand at her white hem in awe that she should seem to shower them with blossoms, eternally offering what she could never give, inexplicably so stern.
written_by_H016.Excerpt2: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between craving something and fulfillment. Sometimes I want something so much I feel like I’m going to break open. Let’s say it’s a fresh berry, let’s say it’s like I’ve been really wanting a fresh berry, plucked from a bush in the orchard, even before that berry’s in my hands, it’s already got a taste in my mind, I’ve been building it up moment after moment until I have it in my brain like I’ve already got it on my tongue, so when Sylvie tells me she picked something for me and plops it in my mouth, it’s even sweeter because the sweetness confirms the foundation I’ve already built for it. I don’t know how to put it. Sylvie disappeared for a while, like a mouse, but then she came back. Sometimes she still goes out though, vanishes into the woods without saying anything. I think she’s out there right now, watching me ruminate. I don’t know what kind of solitude we can both get when we both are in each other’s minds. Could it be a way of being together? A very strange way? It’s beautiful out in the woods. The trees are older than I can fathom, really, old like stories can be old. I’d like to put a status out there, almost like somebody would always be watching, a statue of a woman, to stand in between all those old trees, a woman in a crown of new flowers, looking only ever ahead, forward, never letting any kind of barrenness touch her, like she was the opposite of Lot’s wife and all there was to her was the kind of forgiving vibrancy that children wonder at, the vibrancy that comes from a life well-lived. Even as a statue, I think they’d come to her, every child that’s ever felt lost-wild and orphan, and I think when they’d reach out to touch her stone hands, they’d find that that statue’s stone was warm for them. Sometimes I wish Sylvie were warmer. There’s warmth all around in all the beautiful trees and even the grasses. The problem is that trees don’t feel warm when you touch their bark unless it’s from the sun.

written_by_H016.Original: To crave and to have are as like as a thing and its shadow. For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it, and when is the taste refracted into so many hues and savors of ripeness and earth, and when do our senses know any thing so utterly as when we lack it? And here again is a foreshadowing—the world will be made whole. For to wish for a hand on one’s hair is all but to feel it. So whatever we may lose, very craving gives it back to us again. Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries.Sylvie was gone. She had left without a word, or a sound. I thought she must be teasing, perhaps watching me from the woods. I pretended not to know I was alone. I could see why Sylvie thought children might come here. Any child who saw once how the gleaming water spilled to the tips of branches, and rounded and dropped and pocked the softening shadows of frost at the foot of each tree, would come to see it again.If there had been snow I would have made a statue, a woman to stand along the path, among the trees. The children would have come close, to look at her. Lot’s wife was salt and barren, because she was full of loss and mourning, and looked back. But here rare flowers would gleam in her hair, and on her breast, and in her hands, and there would be children all around her, to love and marvel at her for her beauty, and to laugh at her extravagant adornments, as if they had set the flowers in her hair and thrown down all the flowers at her feet, and they would forgive her, eagerly and lavishly, for turning away, though she never asked to be forgiven. Though her hands were ice and did not touch them, she would be more than mother to them, she so calm, so still, and they such wild and orphan things.

written_by_H011.Excerpt2: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Sylvie had said earlier that in springtime we could pick berries here. I searched for Sylvie's hand beside mine, but I found that she had slipped away silently and left me alone in the clearing. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. Again I looked for Sylvie and thought of how I was, in searching for someone who had left me, not unlike the poor woman who had been turned to salt. Unlike the taste of those imagined berries, I was not sure if my longing for connection could ever be quite enough to evoke the presence of the thing itself.
